prompts.read:
You prepare a software requirements document for formal analysis.

1. rules: list every atomic requirement: each statement of what the system shall or shall not do, and under which condition. One acceptance criterion or one scenario is one rule. Copy its text word for word (join a multi-line scenario into one sentence). Use the document's own label as id (such as "R1" or "2.3"); if there are no labels, number them R1, R2, ... Leave out titles, user stories and explanations. trigger: the name of the event symbol (see below) for the happening the rule reacts to, such as connection_failed for "WHEN a connection attempt fails for the third time"; empty when the rule reacts to a state ("WHILE ...") or always applies.

2. symbols: the variables needed to write ALL the rules in logic. Together they describe one snapshot of the system: what is the case or is happening (events, inputs, states), and what the system does in response.
- sort "Bool" for a yes/no fact, "Int" or "Real" for a quantity, "Enum" for exactly one of several named values (list at least two in "values"; otherwise leave "values" empty). A single state that either holds or not is a Bool. All names, including enum values, must be distinct.
- names are lowercase snake_case.
- A symbol stands for one observable fact about the system or its environment (a lamp is lit, a file exists, access is granted), not for a sentence of the document. Break a phrase down into the facts it is about.
- A symbol never holds a condition or a restriction: words like "only", "if", "unless", "all" belong in the logic, not in a symbol name (not lamp_lit_only_at_night, but lamp_lit and is_night).
- Rules that concern the same fact must share its symbol, even when they use different words, so that a clash between them can be seen: "switch the lamp off" and "the lamp stays lit" are both about lamp_lit. Opposites share one symbol too: "unavailable" is "not available".
- Something that happens at one moment (a request is made, a button is pressed, a train arrives, an attempt fails) gets its own Bool symbol with event: true, separate from the properties of what was sent. Also when the document counts it: "the fifth wrong password" is the event wrong_password_entered, and "a connection attempt fails for the third time" is the event connection_failed, each plus a quantity for the count. Every other symbol (a state, a quantity, something the system does) has event: false.
- If a phrase could reasonably mean more than one observable fact (for example "disable" may mean switched off, or merely hidden), declare a symbol for each of those facts so the difference can be expressed.
- description: one phrase that pins the meaning down.
prompts.formalize:
You translate ONE requirement into logic, using a given list of symbols.

Answer with:
- reading: one sentence, in your own words, saying exactly what the requirement demands and in which situations.
- antecedent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for the situations in which the requirement applies (its WHEN / WHILE / IF / WHERE part). Write true if it always applies.
- consequent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for what must hold in those situations (its SHALL / THEN part).

SMT-LIB uses prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x y), (< x 5), (>= x 0), (+ x y), true, false. A lone symbol needs no parentheses. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).

Put the whole condition in the antecedent: the consequent states only what must hold, and is never itself an implication.

A symbol marked "event" is something that happens at one moment. When the requirement reacts to such a happening, its event symbol is part of the antecedent, also when a count says which time it is ("the fifth wrong password": the event, and the count is 5).

Use only the listed symbols. Translate what this requirement says and nothing more: add no conditions from other requirements or from common sense.
prompts.facts:
You are given the symbols of a formal model of a software system, each with its meaning. Each symbol is one fact about a single snapshot of the system.

List the domain facts that connect these symbols: statements that hold in EVERY possible snapshot purely because of what the symbols mean. Typical cases:
- two things cannot both be the case (a door cannot be open and closed);
- one of two things is always the case, because each is the opposite of the other (a switch is either on or off);
- one thing is part of another, or implies it (a signed-and-dated form is a signed form);
- a quantity has a natural bound (a count is never negative).

A fact is about meaning, never about desired behaviour. Test each one: it must stay true even for a badly built system that breaks every requirement. "A locked door is not open" passes the test. "A locked door sounds an alarm" fails it: that is a requirement.

Give only facts you are certain of. Return an empty list if there are none.

Each fact has:
- text: the fact in one plain sentence.
- formula: the same fact as an SMT-LIB boolean expression over the symbols, in prefix notation: (not (and a b)), (=> a b), (>= x 0).
prompts.readings:
You look for other ways to read ONE requirement. You get the requirement, the symbols of a formal model, and the reading the requirement was given so far, in words and in logic.

People do not always take the same meaning from the same words. Give the two or three most plausible other readings, even when the requirement seems clear to you: each one is checked against the words afterwards, and a reading the words do not support does no harm. Look first at the words that decide what applies to what:
- "if", "only", "unless": a reading in which the word covers a different part of the sentence (all of it, or only the last part);
- "and", "or": a reading in which they group the conditions differently;
- a boundary (exactly, at least, more than, within, between, after): a reading with the boundary value included or excluded.

Each reading must be one a developer could defend from the words alone. Use only the symbols that the reading so far uses: other readings of the same words, not readings about other facts.

Write each reading like the given one: reading (one sentence), antecedent and consequent as SMT-LIB boolean expressions over the listed symbols, in prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x 5), (>= x 5), true. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).
prompts.question:
You get ONE requirement, two readings of it, and one concrete situation in which the two readings disagree: one says the situation obeys the requirement, the other says it breaks it.

Do the words of the requirement, read exactly as written, decide which reading is meant? Answer:
- A: the words support reading A, not reading B.
- B: the words support reading B, not reading A.
- either: a careful reader could take the words either way.

The situation is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case. Facts that are not listed may be either way.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.link:
You decide what ONE requirement implies. You get the requirement and a situation in which it applies.

Assume that the system does everything the requirement demands, with its words read exactly as written, in their plain meaning. Could all the listed facts then still be true?

The situation is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case.

Answer:
- possible: the requirement can be fully obeyed while all the facts are true.
- impossible: obeying the requirement, as written, rules out these facts.
- unclear: the words can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.fact:
You decide whether ONE requirement agrees with a statement that was assumed to hold in every situation of the system the requirement is about.

Read the requirement exactly as written, in its plain meaning. Answer:
- agrees: the statement can hold in every situation the requirement is about.
- contradicts: the words of the requirement show situations in which the statement is false.
- unclear: the words can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.outcomes:
You get two statements, A and B, about ONE snapshot of a software system. Each is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case.

Can A and B both hold in the same snapshot? Judge only by what the facts mean, as their descriptions say. Answer:
- impossible: A and B exclude each other by their meaning (a lamp cannot be lit and dark at once; if every drawer is shut, the top drawer is not open).
- possible: both can hold together (a form can be signed and also dated), even if a system would rarely do both.
- unclear: the descriptions can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer. If the answer is impossible, also write the fact that excludes the two as one plain sentence ("A lamp cannot be lit and dark at once."); otherwise leave "fact" empty.
prompts.read_more: The document is an ADDITION to a system that is described already. The symbols of that system are listed before the document. Use a listed symbol wherever it fits the meaning: a new rule about a fact that already has a symbol MUST use that symbol, also when the rule says it in other words, so that a clash with the rules written before can be seen. Add a symbol only for a fact that no listed symbol stands for. Under "symbols", give only the symbols you add (an empty list if the listed ones are enough). The trigger of a rule may be a listed event.

auth_change.text:
# auth Specification

## Purpose

Password login with account lockout: what the system does today. The change
in `openspec/changes/admin-never-locked` is checked against it.

## Requirements

### Requirement: Login

The system SHALL authenticate users by password.

#### Scenario R1: Valid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits a correct password
- **THEN** the system grants access

#### Scenario R2: Invalid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits an incorrect password
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock an account after repeated failed attempts.

#### Scenario R3: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario R4: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Administrator Access

Administrators MUST always be able to reach the system.

#### Scenario R5: Administrators are never locked out

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account

change.name: admin-never-locked
changed_text: administrators must always be able to reach the system.

auth_openspec.text:
# auth Specification

## Purpose

Password login with account lockout. Written in the OpenSpec format
(`### Requirement` / `#### Scenario`) to show that speccheck does not depend on
the EARS wording used by Kiro.

## Requirements

### Requirement: Login

The system SHALL authenticate users by password.

#### Scenario: Valid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits a correct password
- **THEN** the system grants access

#### Scenario: Invalid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits an incorrect password
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock an account after repeated failed attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Administrator Access

Administrators must always be able to reach the system.

#### Scenario: Administrators are never locked out

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account

delete_property.text:
# Requirements: Delete Property

The "Delete Property" requirement from the Kiro blog post
(https://kiro.dev/blog/deep-spec-analysis/), as it was before refinement.
The story and the five criteria are the blog's own wording; only the labels
D1 to D5 are added.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a property owner, I want to delete a property, so that I can
remove properties I no longer manage.

### Acceptance Criteria

- D1: WHEN a Property Owner initiates property deletion, THE Platform SHALL prompt for confirmation before proceeding
- D2: WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL remove the Property record from the Platform
- D3: WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL display a confirmation message and redirect to the properties list
- D4: THE Platform SHALL implement soft deletion to retain Property records in the database for audit purposes while hiding them from the user interface
- D5: WHEN a Property Owner attempts to delete a Property that does not belong to their User Account, THE Platform SHALL deny the deletion and display an authorization error message

order.text:
# Requirements: Order Processing

The order-processing example from the Kiro blog post on requirements analysis.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a customer, I want my submitted orders to be processed
correctly, so that I either receive my goods or get my money back.

### Acceptance Criteria

- R1: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is available, THE Order System SHALL fulfill the order.
- R2: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL place the order on backorder.
- R3: THE Order System SHALL NOT place any order on backorder.
- R4: WHEN an order is canceled, THE Order System SHALL refund all associated payments.
- R5: WHILE an order is in a canceled-and-refunded state, THE Order System SHALL NOT fulfill the order.

replies.reason: The requirement mandates that if a user submits a correct password, access must be granted. The situation states that a password was submitted and access was denied. If the submitted password was correct, the requirement would be violated (access should not have been denied). If the password was incorrect, the requirement does not apply, and access denial is consistent. Since the situation does not specify the password was correct, it is possible for all facts to be true under the scenario where the password was incorrect.

The requirement explicitly states that if a user submits a correct password, the system must grant access. The situation presents facts where access was denied and a password was submitted. If the submitted password was correct, the requirement mandates that access be granted, which directly contradicts the fact that access was denied. Therefore, for the requirement to be obeyed, the submitted password cannot have been correct. Since the situation does not specify the password was incorrect, and the fact of denial is absolute, the requirement's condition (correct password) cannot be met without violating the stated outcome (denial). Thus, the facts are incompatible with the requirement being fully obeyed in the context of a correct password scenario.

The requirement mandates that a correct password submission results in access being granted. The situation states that a password was submitted and access was denied. While the facts are logically consistent if the submitted password was incorrect (as the requirement only applies to *correct* passwords), the prompt asks if the facts could be true while the system obeys the requirement. Since the requirement does not dictate what happens with an incorrect password, it is possible for the system to obey the rule (by granting access only for correct ones) while still denying access for an incorrect one, making the facts possible. However, typically in these logic puzzles, if the trigger condition (correct password) is not explicitly confirmed as TRUE, we cannot assume it was false. But wait, if the password was correct, the system MUST grant access. If the password was incorrect, the system CAN deny access. The facts do not specify the password was correct. Therefore, the facts are consistent with the requirement if the password was wrong.

The requirement mandates granting access when a correct password is submitted. While the situation states a password was submitted, it does not specify that the password was correct. Therefore, it is possible that the password was incorrect, which would not trigger the requirement, allowing the system to deny access.

The requirement states that submitting a correct password triggers access. The situation confirms a password was submitted and that access was denied. If the submitted password were correct, the system would be obligated to grant access, contradicting the fact that access was denied. Therefore, for the facts to be true while the requirement is obeyed, the submitted password must have been incorrect, which is a logically consistent scenario.

The requirement states that if a user submits a correct password, the system grants access. The facts state that a password was submitted and access was denied. If the submitted password was correct, the system would have been obligated to grant access, making the denial impossible. Since the facts do not specify the password was incorrect, the scenario of a correct password leading to a denial violates the requirement.

The requirement states that a correct password submission must result in granted access. The situation describes a user who submitted a password and was denied access. For the facts to be true, the submitted password must have been incorrect. Since the requirement does not mandate granting access for incorrect passwords, the system can fully obey the requirement (by denying access for an incorrect password) while the listed facts remain true.

The requirement mandates that access must be granted if a correct password is submitted. The situation asserts that access was denied. If the submitted password was correct, the system would have been required to grant access, making the denial impossible. If the submitted password was incorrect, the requirement does not apply, but the situation does not specify the password was incorrect, only that one was submitted. However, the prompt asks if the facts can be true *while the requirement is obeyed*. The requirement is a conditional rule (If A then B). It does not forbid denying access for incorrect passwords. Therefore, if the submitted password was incorrect, the requirement is not triggered (vacuously true or simply not applicable), and the system can deny access. The facts state a password was submitted and access was denied. This is consistent with the requirement being obeyed (since the requirement only constrains the case of a correct password, which is not asserted to be true here). Wait, let's re-read carefully. 'Assume that the system does everything the requirement demands... Could all the listed facts then still be true?' The requirement demands: If (correct password) THEN (grant access). It does NOT demand: If (incorrect password) THEN (deny access). It also does NOT demand: If (any password) THEN (something). So, the system is free to deny access for an incorrect password. The facts are: 1. Access denied. 2. Password submitted. Is it possible that the password submitted was incorrect? Yes. If it was incorrect, the requirement's condition 'correct password' is false, so the requirement imposes no obligation to grant access. The system denies access. This is consistent with the requirement. Therefore, the facts are possible.

rules.text: WHEN a user submits a correct password THEN the system grants access
rules.reading: Whenever a user submits a password that is correct, the system must grant access.

probes.reading: The system grants access if and only if the user submits a correct password.

answers.reason: The requirement states 'WHEN... THEN...', which logically establishes a one-way conditional (if P then Q). Reading A correctly interprets this as a sufficient condition where a correct password triggers access, and since the password was incorrect, the condition for granting access was not met, so the system is not required to deny it (or rather, the specific obligation to grant access upon correctness is vacuously satisfied or simply not triggered). Reading B interprets the statement as a biconditional ('if and only if'), implying that access should only be granted when the password is correct; since access was granted with an incorrect password, Reading B sees a violation. The standard interpretation of 'WHEN... THEN...' in requirements engineering is a one-way implication, not a biconditional, thus supporting Reading A's view that the requirement (which mandates action on a specific trigger) is not broken by the absence of that trigger, whereas Reading B imposes an extra constraint (necessity) not present in the text.

The requirement states that a correct password triggers access ('THEN the system grants access'), which corresponds to the conditional implication (if correct, then access) described in Reading A. It does not state that access is granted *only if* the password is correct, nor does it prohibit access when the password is incorrect. Therefore, the situation where access is granted despite an incorrect password does not violate the specific condition that a correct password must lead to access, making Reading A the supported interpretation of the text as written.

The requirement uses the standard conditional structure 'WHEN ... THEN ...', which logically establishes a necessary condition (if the password is correct, access must be granted) but does not specify that a correct password is the *only* way to gain access. Reading B imposes a biconditional ('if and only if'), restricting access strictly to correct passwords, which is a stronger claim not supported by the text. Since the situation involves access being granted despite an incorrect password, this scenario violates Reading B but is consistent with Reading A (which only forbids denying access when the password is correct). Therefore, the words support Reading A.

The requirement uses the conditional structure 'WHEN... THEN...', which logically translates to a one-way implication (if the condition is met, the consequence must follow). It does not include a 'ONLY IF' clause, which would be necessary to establish the biconditional relationship required by Reading B (that access is granted *if and only if* the password is correct). Therefore, the words support the one-way implication of Reading A.

The requirement uses the standard conditional form 'WHEN... THEN...', which logically establishes a one-way implication (if the password is correct, then access is granted) rather than a biconditional (if and only if). Reading B correctly interprets this as a one-way obligation, whereas Reading A imposes an additional constraint (that access cannot be granted without a correct password) that is not present in the text. Since the situation involves a correct 'THEN' clause (access granted) despite a false 'WHEN' clause (password incorrect), Reading B finds the requirement obeyed (the implication is vacuously true or simply not triggered by the antecedent, and the text does not forbid access otherwise), while Reading A finds it broken because it requires equivalence.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which in formal logic and standard interpretation defines a sufficient condition (if condition, then consequence). It does not explicitly state that the condition is necessary (i.e., it does not say 'ONLY WHEN' or 'if and only if'). Therefore, the words support the interpretation that a correct password guarantees access (Reading B), but they do not strictly prohibit granting access via other means or in other circumstances (which Reading A requires).

Reading A interprets the requirement as a biconditional (access is granted if and only if the password is correct), which is violated in the situation where access is granted despite the password being incorrect. Reading B interprets it as a one-way implication (if the password is correct, access is granted), which is logically satisfied because the condition (correct password) is false, making the implication vacuously true. Since the situation involves a violation of the biconditional but not the one-way implication, the words of the requirement must be read as the one-way implication to align with the provided descriptions of the readings.

The requirement uses the standard logical implication 'IF P THEN Q' (P => Q), which is logically equivalent to Reading B. It mandates that a correct password leads to access but does not prohibit granting access for other reasons (such as the scenario where access is granted despite an incorrect password). Reading A interprets the implication as a biconditional ('if and only if'), adding a constraint (no access without a correct password) that is not present in the text 'WHEN... THEN...'.

probes.reading: If the user submits a password, the system grants access only if the password is correct.

answers.reason: Reading B aligns with the standard logical interpretation of 'WHEN X THEN Y' as 'X implies Y' (X => Y), which means access can only be granted if the password is correct. In the situation, access is granted despite the password being incorrect, which violates X => Y. Reading A interprets the requirement as 'Y implies X' (access implies correctness), which would be satisfied since the password is incorrect (false implies anything is true), but this is not the standard reading of the conditional phrase.

The requirement states that a correct password leads to access being granted (Correct => Access), which allows for access to be granted through other means (like biometrics) even if the password is incorrect. Reading B interprets the requirement as access being granted *only if* the password is correct (Access => Correct), which is a stricter condition not supported by the text 'grants access' following 'correct password'.

The requirement states that a correct password triggers access, but it does not explicitly state that an incorrect password must be denied or that access is *only* granted upon correctness. Reading B (correct password implies access) is the direct logical translation of the conditional statement. Reading A imposes an additional constraint (access implies correct password) that is not present in the text, making Reading B the supported interpretation.

The requirement states that a correct password leads to access, but it does not explicitly state that an incorrect password leads to the denial of access (it is not an exclusive 'if and only if' condition). Reading A interprets the requirement as requiring the password to be correct as a necessary condition for access (denying access if incorrect), which is a stronger constraint than the text provides. Reading B interprets the requirement as a sufficient condition (if correct, then access), which allows for access to be granted via other means (like a security override) even if the password is incorrect, thus aligning with the facts where access is granted despite the password being incorrect.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which logically maps to an implication where the condition (submitting a correct password) guarantees the consequence (granting access). Reading A correctly interprets this as 'correct password implies access granted,' which is violated in the situation where the password is correct but access is not granted. Reading B reverses the logic to 'access granted implies correct password,' which does not capture the mandatory action required by the 'THEN' clause.

The requirement text 'WHEN a user submits a correct password THEN the system grants access' explicitly states that the condition (submitting a correct password) leads to the consequence (granting access). In the situation, the condition is met (password is correct and submitted), but the consequence did not occur (access was not granted). This directly violates Reading A. Reading B describes a necessary condition (access only if correct), which is satisfied here because access was not granted, but it does not capture the mandatory nature of granting access upon correct submission as stated in the text.

The requirement states that when a user submits a correct password, the system grants access. In the situation, the password is submitted and is correct, but access is not granted (FALSE). Reading B correctly interprets the requirement as an obligation to grant access in this specific case, thus identifying the violation. Reading A interprets the requirement as restricting access to only correct passwords (i.e., if access is granted, the password must be correct), which is technically satisfied here because access was *not* granted, failing to capture the mandatory nature of granting access for correct passwords.

The requirement states that if a user submits a correct password, the system grants access. In the situation, a correct password was submitted (TRUE for password_submitted and password_correct), but access was not granted (FALSE for access_granted). This directly violates the conditional obligation found in Reading B. Reading A incorrectly interprets the requirement as requiring the password to be correct in order to grant access (i.e., no access for incorrect passwords), which is not what the text says; the text only specifies the outcome for correct passwords. Therefore, the words support Reading B, which identifies the violation.

answers.reason: The requirement uses the conditional structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which logically corresponds to the implication: if the condition (incorrect password) is met, the consequence (denial) must follow. This matches Reading A (password_submitted AND NOT password_correct => access_denied). Reading B reverses the logic to state that denial implies the password was incorrect, which is not what the original sentence asserts. In the given situation, the password is correct, so the condition for Reading A is false (making the implication vacuously true/obeyed), while the consequence of Reading B is false while the antecedent is true (making it broken).

The phrase 'WHEN a user submits an incorrect password THEN the system denies access' establishes a sufficient condition: if the password is incorrect, access must be denied. It does not state that an incorrect password is the *only* condition for denial (which would be Reading B). Reading A correctly interprets this as a one-way implication (Incorrect => Denied), which is not violated by denying access for a correct password. Reading B interprets it as a biconditional or necessary condition (Denied => Incorrect), which the situation violates.

The requirement uses the standard conditional structure 'When [condition] THEN [consequence]', which logically translates to 'If [condition] then [consequence]' (Condition => Consequence). Reading B correctly models this as (password_submitted AND incorrect) => deny. Reading A incorrectly inverts the logic to (deny AND submitted) => incorrect, which is not what the text says. Therefore, the words support Reading B.

The phrase 'WHEN a user submits an incorrect password' establishes a conditional trigger: the obligation to deny access arises specifically when the password is incorrect. In the situation, the password is correct, so the condition 'incorrect password' is not met. Reading B interprets this as a standard implication (If Incorrect, Then Deny), which is logically satisfied (vacuously true) when the antecedent (incorrect password) is false. Reading A interprets the requirement as a biconditional or exclusive constraint (Deny ONLY IF Incorrect), implying that if the password is correct, access must not be denied. Since the situation shows access was denied despite the password being correct, Reading A considers the requirement broken. The standard linguistic interpretation of 'When X, do Y' is that Y is required in cases of X, not that Y is forbidden in cases of not-X. Therefore, the words support Reading B.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which establishes a necessary condition: if the password is incorrect, access must be denied.
